drills.q: What is the span naming convention for a chat completion call, and what does it look like for a call to Anthropic?
drills.a: {operation} {gen_ai.system}, so a chat call to Anthropic is named 'chat anthropic'.

drills.q: Is prompt/completion content captured by default in OTel GenAI instrumentation? What controls it?
drills.a: No, off by default. Controlled by the OTEL_INSTRUMENTATION_GENAI_CAPTURE_MESSAGE_CONTENT environment variable, and content goes into span events, not attributes, when enabled.

drills.q: Name the three agent-lifecycle span types in the GenAI conventions.
A colleague wants to add `conversation_id` as a label on a Prometheus-style metric so they can filter dashboards by conversation. What's wrong with this, and what should they do instead?
drills.a: conversation_id is unbounded, so it creates unbounded time series (cardinality explosion), inflating cost and degrading the backend. Keep conversation_id as a span/trace attribute only; use exemplars to drill from a metric into a specific trace if the backend supports it.

drills.q: Design the span hierarchy for an agent that takes 3 turns, calling one tool on turn 2. Name each span level.
drills.a: Run span (invoke_agent) at top; 3 step spans as children, one per turn; each step span contains a model span (chat {provider}); the turn-2 step span additionally contains an execute_tool child span. Reasoning goes on each step span as an event.

drills.q: Your team is deciding between head-based and tail-based sampling for a new agent feature's traces. Make the case for tail-based.
drills.a: Head-based sampling decides upfront probabilistically, discarding rare/expensive/erroring traces at the same rate as routine ones. Tail-based decides after the trace completes, letting you keep 100% of errors, 100% of cost outliers (e.g. over $0.50), and sample only routine traffic at 5-20% -- biasing the trace store toward what an incident review actually needs.

drills.q: A trace shows an agent made 14 nearly-identical execute_tool spans before failing, but content capture was off. What can you diagnose, and what can't you, and what would fix the gap?
drills.a: You can see the tool was called 14 times and how long each took, but not whether it was retrying the same failing argument, escalating, or genuinely exploring different approaches -- that needs tool argument/result events, which weren't captured. Fix: enable content capture (redacted or feature-flagged) or add a lightweight error-reason attribute on the tool span even when full args are withheld.

drills.q: Why is hardcoding a per-token dollar price directly into your instrumentation/span-emission code a mistake, even beyond the price going stale?
drills.a: It also can't correctly represent historical cost trends -- if prices change, spans emitted after the change report the new price against old requests unless the price table is versioned with effective-date ranges and looked up per span timestamp downstream, not baked in at emission.

drills.q: Your gen_ai.usage.input_tokens numbers don't match the provider's billing dashboard. Walk through the debugging steps.
drills.a: First check whether the convention's cached+uncached combined definition is being double-counted against a separately reported cache-token line item in your cost pipeline. Reconcile against the provider's own usage/billing API directly. If still mismatched, check whether retried requests (each a full token-consuming call) are being summed across every model span in a trace, not just the last successful one.

drills.q: Your org runs OpenInference-instrumented code (Arize's convention) alongside OTel-GenAI-instrumented code, and the same underlying concept (token usage) shows up under two different attribute keys in different spans of the same trace. How do you fix this without rewriting either instrumentation library?
drills.a: Add a normalization step in the OTel Collector -- an attribute-processor rule that maps OpenInference keys to OTel GenAI keys (or vice versa) at ingestion, so downstream dashboards and queries see one consistent vocabulary regardless of which library produced the raw span.

drills.q: A single-call LLM feature (one prompt, one completion, no tools) is about to get a tool added. At what point should you refactor from a single span to the full run/step/tool hierarchy, and why not wait longer?
drills.a: Refactor as soon as there's a second decision point or a tool call that can itself fail or branch -- that's exactly when 'why did it do that' becomes a real question a flat single span can't answer. Waiting for a second or third tool means shipping blind through the first incident that needs that visibility.
